Every crisis since 2020, from the COVID crash to the Terra and FTX crashes and the SVB collapse, has tested whether holders trust stablecoins, and the market capitalization of stablecoins has recovered after each crisis.

These crises have also shown which designs can withstand the test. Terra, which relies on algorithms rather than reserves...

UST crashed, while the two major stablecoins, USDT and USDC, primarily backed by cash and US Treasury bonds, currently account for 86% of the stablecoin market capitalization. Most tokenized stocks use the same reserve-backed design. https://tokenterminal.com/explorer/tokenized-assets/stablecoins The market capitalization of tokenized stocks is now comparable to that of stablecoins in March 2020, and tokenized stocks reached this level much faster. From the moment their respective market capitalizations surpassed $1 billion, tokenized stocks took 8 months to reach $4.8 billion, while stablecoins took 11 months. Tokenized stocks are also emerging in a more mature market, with wallets, exchanges, and DeFi venues already in place, and the regulatory environment is clearer than that of stablecoins in 2020, including an SEC exemption for tokenized stock trading starting in September 2026. src="https://img.jinse.com.cn/7523606_watermarknone.png" alt="Why is the 'next stablecoin moment' said to be tokenized stocks?" " preview="3" data-pswp-uid="3">

https://tokenterminal.com/docs/mcp/introduction

The demand served by tokenized stocks is enormous. Foreign investors hold $25.2 trillion in US stocks, which has grown by 23% in the past 12 months, while the market capitalization of tokenized stocks is only equivalent to 0.02% of foreign holdings. If 1% of foreign-held US stocks were moved on-chain, the scale would reach $252 billion, approximately 50 times the current tokenized stock market.

https://tokenterminal.com/docs/mcp/introduction

2. The US has the same interests in tokenized stocks as it does in stablecoins

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has stated that stablecoins could become one of the largest buyers of US Treasury bonds and help expand the dollar's influence overseas. Tokenized stocks can play the same role as US stocks, and four characteristics of the tokenized stock market demonstrate this parallel: the assets are US, the buyers are foreign, the tokens are backed by real shares, and the majority of the shares are held by US custodians.

Most tokenized stocks track US-listed assets. US-listed stocks and exchange-traded funds (ETFs) account for 88% of the market capitalization of tokenized stocks.

https://tokenterminal.com/explorer/fact-sheets?view=map

Almost all tokenized stocks are backed by real shares. Tokens backed by underlying shares at a 1:1 ratio account for 91% of the market capitalization of tokenized stocks, which is the same structure as stablecoins backed by the US dollar. Therefore, one token sold overseas corresponds to one share purchased in the US market.

https://tokenterminal.com/explorer/tokenized-assets/stocks?stocksReferenceAssets=mstr,strc

3. On-chain use makes tokenized stocks harder to replace

Every new use case for stablecoins, whether in exchanges, lending markets, or payments, makes them more useful to others and harder to replace. Tokenized stocks are beginning to follow the same use case. DeFi TVL, the value of tokenized stocks deposited into on-chain applications such as lending markets and trading pools, has grown 24 times in the past year, reaching $300 million. Currently, deposits represent 6.3% of the market capitalization of tokenized stocks, up from 2.4% a year ago, and each deposit adds liquidity for the next trader and earns yield for the holder.

https://tokenterminal.com/explorer/tokenized-assets/stocks?stocksMetric=asset_tvl

Weekend trading provides holders with another reason to stay on-chain, as US exchanges are closed on Saturdays and Sundays. In October 2026, weekends accounted for 18% of tokenized stock trading volume on decentralized exchanges (DEXs), or $2.4 billion, 83 times the level of a year ago. Holders can act based on the news before the market opens on Monday.

https://tokenterminal.com/explorer/tokenized-assets/stocks?stocksMetric=asset_trading_volume

4. Restrictions on asset-backed tokens will drive demand to perpetual futures marketplaces

A key risk of tokenized stocks comes from regulation. If US regulators restrict tokenized stocks backed 1:1 by shares, demand for US stocks in non-US markets is likely to shift to perpetual futures (perps), which are price-tracking contracts with no expiration date and no underlying stock.

The stock perpetual futures market is already growing. Trade.xyz is a perpetual futures exchange built on Hyperliquid.

The perpetual futures market is already growing.

It's a blockchain designed for trading, and the exchange has launched US stock and index contracts. The open interest in Trade.xyz's stock perpetual contracts—the value of open positions—has grown 55 times in the past year, reaching $1.54 billion. Each position in a perpetual contract doesn't require an underlying stock, so less of the demand moving to perpetual contracts ultimately ends up in US stocks and US custodians, and perpetual contracts don't pay dividends that are taxable in the US. Supporting asset-backed tokens allows more overseas demand to remain in US stocks. " preview="13" data-pswp-uid="13">

https://tokenterminal.com/explorer/projects/tradexyz/xyzspcx?metric1=open-interest

Core Conclusions

Today's tokenized stocks look like stablecoins in 2020. Tokenized stocks use the same reserve-backed design, grew their market capitalization from $1 billion to $4.8 billion much faster, and relied on $25.2 trillion in overseas holdings of US stocks. This gives the US the same reason to support tokenized stocks as it does to support stablecoins, because restricting asset-backed tokens would push the same overseas demand toward perpetual contracts, where less demand would reach US stocks.

data.title: How to protect your wealth during geopolitical storms?
data.description:
Author: Christina Comben; Translator: Chopper, Foresight News

Geopolitical conflicts, cyberattacks, and power grid failures could strike at any time, and more and more governments are beginning to remind their citizens to prepare for major disasters.

In the UK, people are responding to the government's "Be Ready" campaign by stockpiling canned food and bottled water.

Fighter jets flying over the Middle East, rumors of a dirty bomb attack on Washington, D.C., and the world's largest software company experiencing a full-day outage—the possibility of disaster hitting our doorstep is becoming increasingly real.

But what about your money then? How can you protect your wealth while ensuring access to it in case of system failure?

The key lies in two things: choosing assets that will retain their value even if the world is engulfed in flames, and having access to funds in an emergency.

Regarding the first point, Maximilian Kunkel, Chief Investment Officer for Ultra-High Net Worth Clients at UBS, one of the world's largest wealth management firms, told Magazine, "We want to remind you not to assume that any single asset is safe in all circumstances." He said wealthy investors should focus on building a portfolio that is "resilient across multiple scenarios," has sufficient liquidity, and is well-diversified across asset classes, currencies, and geographies. The Boundaries Between Bitcoin, Gold, and "Safe-Haven Assets" UBS's 2026 Global Family Office Report covers families with an average net worth of $2.7 billion, of which 64% listed major geopolitical conflicts as their biggest concern for the next 12 months. However, these investors have not flocked to the cryptocurrency market in an attempt to preserve their wealth. "24% of family offices report exposure to cryptocurrencies or digital assets, but within those investments, the allocation is typically only around 1%," explains Hadley Stern, head of institutional business at Silence Laboratories and founder of Fidelity Digital Assets. He adds that financial institutions may now classify Bitcoin and gold in the same category, but Bitcoin hasn't yet gained the same safe-haven reputation. "Gold has been around for thousands of years… Bitcoin is less than twenty. But the logic is the same: a scarce asset that isn't a liability to any other party," he says. He advised against using it as a reliable hedge during a crisis: "I'm a bit cautious about the term 'hedge,'" he said. "Bitcoin remains highly volatile and often trades alongside other risky assets during market sell-offs." In contrast, cash is useful in emergencies but not suitable for "long-term preservation of value," he said. Michael D'Alessio, COO of digital asset trading platform Talos, told Magazine that there are early signs that Bitcoin is beginning to resemble gold more. He said that during the period of volatility surrounding the US midterm elections, Bitcoin's correlation with stocks remained high; however, its correlation with gold also increased significantly during the same period, reaching approximately 0.75 over a 30-day period as of early August. "This is a significant shift, and it's exactly the kind of signal institutional investors are now looking for." [Image: 30-day rolling daily yield correlation between Bitcoin and gold. Source: Talos / Coin Metrics] The risk isn't just losing money, it's not being able to withdraw it. The collapse of Mt. Gox, and more recently, the collapse of a Paraguayan bank, demonstrates that "the safety of an asset depends on the system that holds it," Stern said. Instead of automatically turning to Bitcoin or gold when tensions escalate, the risk committees within these institutions are starting to ask other questions: "Where are the assets? In which jurisdiction? Who can freeze them? What if counterparties or payment channels are shut down for a week?" he said. "These used to be back-office questions, but now they're being discussed at the board level." Kunkel said concerns about major geopolitical conflicts are prompting wealthy families to consider "not just asset allocation, but also where to put assets, currency exposure, liquidity, and jurisdictional diversification." A UBS report found that 88% of family offices hold depository assets in two or more jurisdictions, and 30% are increasing or considering increasing currency diversification. The institutional version of "filling storage rooms" is a good thing. Fortunately, banks and custodians are also making actual disaster preparedness plans. "Regulators expect institutions to plan for 'serious but reasonable' events," Stern explained, such as cloud service outages, cyberattacks, the collapse of key suppliers, or market closures for several days, and to "prove they can maintain the most critical services in these situations." The UK government advises the public to stockpile supplies. Source: Gov.uk

For custodians, this means testing: if a signing location goes offline, can assets still be transferred? If a data center is gone, how quickly can operations recover? Stern says that while families might fill their storage rooms to prepare for emergencies, the institutional approach is: not relying on any single thing—not relying on a single custodian, a single key holder, a single cloud service, or a single bank.

Similarly, investors need to figure out which assets can be withdrawn quickly and which cannot, and "maintain enough liquidity to weather a bad period without being forced to sell."

Kunkel says that capital preservation "does not mean eliminating volatility, but maintaining enough liquidity and diversification to withstand volatility," avoiding becoming a forced seller.

When something truly serious happens, diversification can protect a portfolio from market shocks, but if the infrastructure supporting it fails, you may not be able to access your funds.

Hedging is not just about owning the right things; it's about having access to them even when the system crashes.

data.title: Anthropic's stock price nearly fell below its IPO price on its second day of trading: The underwriting syndicate is under pressure.
data.description:
Author: Gao Zhimou, Wall Street Insights

Anthropic announced Friday morning that the "greenshoe" option (over-allotment option) for its IPO had been exercised. With this option exercised, subsequent market support measures have decreased. Furthermore, approximately 300 million Anthropic shares will become tradable on December 15th, potentially leading to further selling pressure.

The largest IPO in history experienced a sharp sell-off on its second day of trading.

Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic (ANT) plunged as much as 15% intraday on Friday, reaching a low of just 5 cents above its IPO price, before closing down 8.5% at $88.91, wiping out approximately $109 billion in market capitalization in a single day.

... This violent market shakeup dashed market expectations that Anthropic could reverse the AI ​​sector's downward trend. On Friday, core AI stocks such as Nvidia, Meta, and Oracle fell in tandem with Anthropic, wiping out $4 trillion in Nasdaq market capitalization. The market turmoil also affected Anthropic's main competitor, OpenAI, which is pushing forward with a new round of massive funding valuing the company at $1.25 trillion and is eager to go public next year. However, sources close to Anthropic and its lead underwriters insist that the IPO was still a success, emphasizing that the company raised over $100 billion through the IPO and concurrent share offering, and held above the offering price even during one of the most intense market sell-offs in history, with Friday's closing price still 7% higher than the offering price.

The allocation favored existing shareholders, with 60% of participating institutions leaving empty-handed

Anthropic showed signs of weakness on its first day of trading.

Before noon on Thursday, the stock opened at more than 30% above its offering price, but buying enthusiasm quickly waned, and it trended lower throughout the day, ultimately closing up 17%.

Some investors questioned the company's and investment banks' allocation arrangements for the $81 billion IPO shares. According to sources, more than half of the IPO shares went to existing investors who already held company equity, including Altimeter Capital, Lightspeed Venture Partners, and Menlo Ventures.

This unusually high proportion reflects Anthropic executives' willingness to reward early backers. Some of these early backers are venture capital firms whose existing holdings are subject to lock-up periods. According to industry practice, venture capital firms typically do not receive large allocations of new shares in an IPO, as these shares can be immediately sold on the secondary market to lock in profits. Furthermore, sources familiar with the matter stated that Anthropic also allocated a significant proportion of its IPO shares to large investment institutions such as Citadel, leading some unsuccessful investors to speculate that the company prioritized major clients of its Claude model. Normally, listed companies and investment banking advisors carefully screen subscription requests, spending several days selecting the best shareholder list to ensure stable post-IPO share price performance and a stable shareholding structure. However, according to some sources, approximately 60% of the institutions that applied to subscribe at the IPO price received nothing, including a large number of hedge funds and large mutual funds. Many other institutions received only partial allocations—according to the Wall Street Journal, asset management giant BlackRock submitted subscription applications for approximately $10 billion, but ultimately only received about half. The opening price was questioned, and immediate employee cashing out exacerbated selling pressure. Besides the allocation controversy, Wall Street is also scrutinizing the offering price and lock-up arrangements. One hedge fund manager questioned whether the investment banks that helped determine the opening timing and price may have set the opening price too high, creating an irreversible downward momentum. However, delaying the opening also carries risks, as the share price could continue to rise during this period. Meanwhile, Anthropic's IPO included a rare clause allowing some current and former employees to immediately sell approximately 300 million shares, worth about $26 billion at the IPO price. In a typical IPO, employee stock ownership plans usually face a lock-up period of several months. This reduction in shareholding likely increased downward pressure on the stock price. Unlike Wall Street's anxiety, several AI practitioners in San Francisco said they largely ignored the pullback in Anthropic's stock price. They were more focused on another piece of news on Friday—an Anthropic mathematician claimed that Claude had solved the "Millennium Prize Problem," a puzzle that had baffled humanity for 167 years. Many see this as a sign that AI is surpassing human intelligence. Furthermore, these employees stated that even at the current stock price, many Anthropic employees' shares are still worth millions of dollars more than at the beginning of the week. AI Deals in Turmoil, Greenshoe Option Exercised Anthropic and its advisors knew that proceeding with an IPO during the most turbulent AI deal to date was extremely risky, but they never expected to encounter this "perfect storm." Rising borrowing costs for cloud computing companies and the lingering effects of the Nvidia controversy have exacerbated market anxiety in recent weeks. Investors had hoped that Anthropic, a pure AI giant, could turn the tide and revive the market, but this did not happen. From the perspective of the underwriting investment banks, as long as Anthropic's share price did not fall below the IPO price, the listing was still considered a success. However, once the share price fell below the IPO price, a key tool that investment banks could use to stabilize the price became ineffective. Anthropic announced on Friday morning that the "greenshoe" option (over-allotment option) for this IPO had been exercised. The "greenshoe" option allows underwriters to offer investors an additional 15% of the shares issued. Underwriters can then either buy back these shares from the company at the IPO price or repurchase them from the open market to support the share price if it falls below the IPO price. With the option being exercised early, subsequent market support measures have decreased. Furthermore, approximately 300 million Anthropic shares will become tradable on December 15th, potentially leading to further selling pressure.
